Human errors are mistakes made by the person taking measurements. Random errors cause unpredictable variations in readings. Systematic errors produce a consistent bias, often due to a faulty or incorrectly zeroed instrument.

Precision describes how close repeated measurements are to one another; accuracy describes how close a measurement is to the accepted or true value. For example, arrows grouped tightly away from the bullseye are precise but inaccurate, while arrows grouped at the bullseye are both precise and accurate.
The regular rotation of Earth on its axis and its revolution around the Sun can serve as reasonably accurate time standards.
